about: A PROJECT-DEFINED EDITORIAL EQUIVALENT, NOT AN EXTERNAL SYLLABUS. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANY EXAMINING BODY. There is no modern Latin proficiency examination -- core/exam-levels.json records exam 'no modern proficiency exam' for this track -- and nothing here may be attributed to Euroclassica, to its European Curriculum for Latin, or to an ELEX paper: latin/assessment-spec.md states that ELEX is not a four-skill pre-A1-to-C2 ladder and that this project claims no equivalence to it. AND NOTHING IN IT MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO DELE, THE INSTITUTO CERVANTES OR THE PLAN CURRICULAR ABOUT LATIN: they published a Spanish syllabus and have said nothing whatever about this language. READ THE THREE CLAIMS APART. (1) THE POINT SET is derived structurally from core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, this project's restatement of the A1 grammar, function, notion and orthography inventories the Instituto Cervantes publishes behind DELE. That is the strongest thing here and all it establishes is a LEVEL. THE PROXY STANDS IN AN ODD RELATION TO THIS TARGET AND IT IS WORTH NAMING: Spanish is Latin's own descendant, so the proxy is a list of demands made by a daughter of the language being measured. Where the daughter kept the mother's machinery the transfer is exact -- este/ese/aquel descends from hic/iste/ille, and the demonstrative point can be taken over word for word. Where the daughter INNOVATED, the proxy asks for something Latin never had and the demand has to be inverted: Spanish's articles become the fact that Latin has none (LA-A1-ART-01), Spanish's four separate past-tense points become one perfect (LA-A1-V-07), Spanish's written accent becomes the macron, which marks length rather than stress and is therefore a larger demand rather than a smaller one (LA-A1-ORT-03). (2) THE LATIN EXPONENTS are editorial throughout and are this project's judgement and nobody else's. (3) THE COVERAGE NUMBER is a measure of the corpus against this list, and for THIS track it must be read with LA-A1-LEC-01 in front of it. THE CAVEAT IN exam-levels.json IS LOAD-BEARING AND IS CARRIED AS A POINT RATHER THAN A FOOTNOTE. It says CEFR is built around communicative can-do statements, that Latin is learned almost entirely for reading, and that a reading-only ladder would fit Latin better. This inventory therefore enumerates 54 functional points about speaking to a living interlocutor for a language that has none, because the shared spine across all 23 tracks requires it -- and LA-A1-LEC-01 says in the file that this is the wrong construct, following the Sanskrit inventory's precedent of a deliberately uncovered point recording what it cannot measure. Four further points (the Lectio column) enumerate the reading construct the caveat names, and three more (the Testimonium column) enumerate a demand only a DEAD language makes: telling an attested phrase from a modern pedagogical one. That column is where this track is strongest. THE SIX DROPPED PROXY POINTS ARE CHRONOLOGICAL, NOT GRAMMATICAL, WHICH IS UNIQUE IN THIS SERIES. Every other inventory that drops a point drops it because the target language lacks a structure. Latin drops the telephone, television and radio, the internet and e-mail, computing, photography, and the Spanish superscript abbreviation letter. The first five are anachronisms: all 112 lessons declare variety: classical, and a Classical Latin A1 inventory cannot demand a word for a thing that did not exist. WHY A PROXY AT ALL: no awarding body publishes a Latin content syllabus this project has read. NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION: no external search was performed for this file; code/learning/human-languages/BACKLOG.d records the sourcing question as settled and directs that it not be repeated per track (HL-C287, HL-C290).
source: PROJECT-DEFINED. LEVEL PROXY: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, the DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Its own source is https://cvc.cervantes.es/ensenanza/biblioteca_ele/plan_curricular/niveles/02_gramatica_inventario_a1-a2.htm and the sibling function, notion and orthography inventories. Nothing about Latin is attributed to DELE, the Instituto Cervantes or the Plan Curricular. EXAM ENVELOPE: ONE EXISTS AND IT IS PROJECT-DEFINED. Unlike italian/ and portuguese/, the latin/ track ships assessment-spec.md, assessment.json and task-shapes/a1.json, so a project-internal contract does bound this file: assessment.json names a 'Coding Adventures Latin A1 Assessment -- project-defined equivalent' with independent reading, listening, writing and speaking passes at 0.6, six cumulative writing stages, and two timed mocks whose rubrics and answer keys are named as REQUIRED FUTURE ARTIFACTS rather than as evidence. The spec states in its own words that the A1 task inventory existing 'alone is not readiness evidence'. This inventory does not claim otherwise. PROFICIENCY BACKBONE: core/exam-levels.json, tracks.latin -- exam 'no modern proficiency exam', basis 'editorial', mapping 'cefr', with the reading-construct caveat that LA-A1-LEC-01 carries. CORPUS EVIDENCE: every probe was checked mechanically against the atoms declared by the 112 lesson files in code/learning/human-languages/latin/lessons/, which introduce 211 distinct atoms between them -- 86 LEX, 71 ETYMON, 29 PRAGMATICS, 15 GRAMMAR, 6 PHONO, 3 DIALOGUE and 1 TASK. All 112 declare variety: classical and register: neutral. NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION: no external search for a Latin content syllabus was performed for this file. See `about`.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json
anchors.note: This project's restatement of the A1 inventories the Instituto Cervantes publishes behind DELE. The only inventory in this repository that restates a real awarding body's published syllabus, so it is the only one that can lend a LEVEL. It lends a level and never a language -- and here it is a DAUGHTER language of the target, which makes some transfers exact and others inversions.

anchors.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume (2020), A1 descriptors
anchors.note: Public, third-party and language-neutral, and the backbone latin/assessment-spec.md itself names. It can anchor a can-do and never a Latin form. It is also the framework whose communicative shape exam-levels.json's caveat says does not fit a reading language, which is why LA-A1-LEC-01 leans on it to say so.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/latin/ -- 112 lessons across 47 chapters, curriculum.d and chapters.d
anchors.note: Our own work. It is what every probe resolves against and it is finite and auditable, but agreeing with it is not corroboration. Where a point's note says a word is missing, that absence was read out of this directory.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/latin/assessment-spec.md, assessment.json and task-shapes/a1.json
anchors.note: The project-internal contract for this track, which italian/ and portuguese/ do not have. It names Classical Latin as the assessed variety, the reconstructed classical pronunciation as the default model, four independently passed skills at 0.6, and mock rubrics and answer keys as required future artifacts. It bounds what this file may claim and it is not external evidence.

anchors.title: This project's unaided judgement about Latin
anchors.note: Every Latin exponent below. Deciding that Spanish's three article points collapse into the single fact that Latin has none, that its four past-tense points land on one untaught perfect, that its nine punctuation points collapse into the fact that Roman texts had no punctuation at all, and that the telephone and the internet are dropped rather than restated -- all of that is chosen here. It is a working default to be corrected, not a standard.

notTransferred.why: The telephone. All 112 lessons declare variety: classical, and latin/assessment-spec.md names Classical Latin as the assessed variety. A Classical Latin A1 inventory cannot demand a word for an object that did not exist, and inventing a Neo-Latin coinage here would be exactly the kind of unlabelled invention LA-A1-TES-01 credits this track with refusing.

Television and radio. Anachronistic for the same reason. The wider notion, information and communication, is enumerated at LA-A1-NE-33 and the Roman shapes of it -- the letter and the inscription -- are enumerated at LA-A1-NE-34 and LA-A1-ORT-10.

The internet, and dictating an e-mail address. Anachronistic, and the second half of it -- dictating letter by letter -- is a real demand that survives translation and is enumerated at LA-A1-ORT-01 instead.
Computing and new technology. Anachronistic. The mathematical half of the same PCIC section, the notion of number, transfers intact and is at LA-A1-NE-57.
Photography. Anachronistic. The rest of the artistic block transfers -- theatre in particular, which is Roman and is enumerated at LA-A1-NE-64.

Superscript letters in frequent abbreviations. Roman abbreviation is by truncation and by initial (S.P.D., cos., D.M.) and raises nothing; there is no Latin convention to restate this onto. The general abbreviation demand transfers and is at LA-A1-ORT-10.

proxy.note: SIX POINTS DROPPED, AND FIVE OF THEM ARE DROPPED FOR A REASON NO OTHER INVENTORY IN THIS SERIES HAS USED: they are ANACHRONISMS rather than grammatical mismatches. Every other track drops a Spanish point because the target language lacks a structure -- Tamil writes no accent, so the accentuation rules go. Latin drops the telephone, television, the internet, computing and photography because the language as this track teaches it (variety: classical on all 112 lessons) has no referent for them. RESTATING A POINT AROUND THE TARGET LANGUAGE'S MACHINERY IS DERIVING IT, and that rule was applied first everywhere else: the articles Latin has not got, the punctuation Roman texts did not use, the inverted question mark, the gustar frame, the possessive that is a dative case rather than a word -- all restated, none dropped.

communicative-functions.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's 54 A1 function points), the Council of Europe CEFR Companion Volume A1 descriptors, and latin/assessment-spec.md
communicative-functions.note: THE DIMENSION exam-levels.json's CAVEAT SAYS IS THE WRONG ONE FOR THIS TRACK, and it is enumerated anyway because the shared spine requires it. See LA-A1-LEC-01, which is a deliberately uncovered point recording that a communicative function column measures something Latin is not learned for. Within that limit the column is genuinely useful, because it surfaces gaps a reading course still cannot afford: the track can greet, thank, apologise, say please, say yes and say no by chapter 4, and cannot ask anybody to repeat anything at all (LA-A1-F6-05).

grammar.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's grammar, sentence and coordination columns)
grammar.note: Walking the Spanish grammar column surfaced demands no reading of the Latin corpus alone would have named: that non is taught as a word and never attached to a verb, that qui/quae/quod return zero occurrences in a reading course, that twenty-five nouns are cited with their genitives and the genitive's job is never stated, that forty verb paradigms are given and the four conjugations are never named as classes. It does not close, because Latin makes demands Spanish cannot see at all -- the case system, free word order, the accusative-and-infinitive, the enclitic question particle -- and those are enumerated in a Casus column of their own on the project's judgement.

phonology-orthography.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json for the orthographic demands, and latin/pronunciation-reference.md
phonology-orthography.note: Latin and Spanish share an alphabet, so this column is not about a new writing system. What the proxy cannot supply is the two things that make Latin orthography its own subject: the macron, which marks LENGTH where a Spanish accent marks stress and which the corpus writes faithfully and scores in its dictation lessons, and the fact that a modern edition's punctuation, word spacing and capitalisation are all editorial rather than Roman -- which collapses nine proxy punctuation points into one untaught fact. The pronunciation-and-prosody half of the source inventory is not level-split, which is why the proxy's own phonology dimension is partial, and that carries straight through.

lexicon.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's general and specific notion inventories)
lexicon.note: Walked at the granularity of the proxy's numbered subsections. It does not close: which Latin words an A1 reader must hold is what a real Latin syllabus would say, and this project has read none. What the column does show is a corpus with an unusual profile -- roughly forty verbs with full paradigms, twenty-five concrete nouns of house, world, night and table, six colours, six time nouns, and almost nothing social or civic. urbs, liber, amicus, deus, lex and miles are all absent, which for a course whose subject is Rome is the finding this column exists to produce.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding -- an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped, and its note is written as a work queue naming what would close it. Every atom named in every probe was checked mechanically against the 211 atoms the latin track actually introduces; a probe naming an atom that does not exist would report 'not covered' forever and be indistinguishable from real debt, so an id was never invented to fill a point. TWO HABITS ARE NAMED SO THEY ARE NOT HIDDEN GENEROSITIES. First, this track files a great deal under PRAGMATICS and ETYMON rather than LEX -- 29 PRAGMATICS and 71 ETYMON atoms against 86 LEX -- so probing a greeting, a courtesy formula or a time word often names a pragmatics or etymology id. The word IS introduced by that lesson. Second, and more importantly for this track: A VERB LESSON HERE INTRODUCES A PARADIGM, NOT A SENTENCE. sedeo's lesson gives all six present forms; it does not put sedeo in a sentence or give it anything to sit on. So a covered lexical point means the learner can DECLINE OR CONJUGATE the word and very often cannot USE it, and the notes say so wherever it matters. A POINT IS NOT COUNTED AS COVERED WHEN ONLY PART OF WHAT IT NAMES IS TAUGHT: bene without male leaves general evaluation uncovered; cras without hodie and heri leaves the time deictics uncovered; quomodo without ubi leaves the interrogative adverbs uncovered; emo without vendo leaves commerce uncovered. `derivedFrom` records each point's provenance -- the proxy point ids whose demand it answers, or an empty list with `latinSpecific: true`. `anchorIds` records which anchor each point leans on, and the anchor's `kind` says whether that was something read or something decided. Neither field is read by any code; both are carried so the derivation can be audited rather than trusted.

points.label: proper nouns: a personal name, given and asked for
points.note: Marcus and Iulia trade names in chapter 21's scene, on the frame chapter 20 builds.

points.label: place names
points.note: Not one place name is introduced. Roma itself never appears as a word to be learnt, which is a strange absence in a Latin course and an easy one to close.

points.label: common nouns naming periods of time
points.note: dies, nox, mane, vesper, hora, meridies -- six, each with a chapter of its own between 28 and 35. The track's strongest notional block after the verbs.

points.label: gender: how a Latin noun's gender is known, and that it is not guessable from meaning
points.note: The Spanish point is masculine in -o, feminine in -a. Latin's demand is larger and differently shaped -- three genders, five declensions, and gender read off the genitive rather than the nominative -- and the corpus states it only in passing, on manus as a rare feminine in a masculine-looking group and on vesper against vespera. No lesson sets out how gender is known.

points.label: gender by heteronymy: the paired kinship words
points.note: pater/mater and frater/soror, chapter 7.

points.label: number: the plural
points.note: NOT TAUGHT AS A NOUN OPERATION ANYWHERE. The plural exists in the corpus only on verbs (salvete against salve, sedemus against sedeo) and in the frozen plural of the weekdays. Twenty-five nouns are taught in chapters 44 to 47 and not one of them is ever pluralised.

points.label: the dictionary citation: a noun is stored with its genitive, a verb with its infinitive
points.note: domus, domus; terra, terrae; sum, esse; dico, dicere. EVERY noun and verb in this track is headed by its citation pair, without exception, which is exactly the habit a reader needs to use a dictionary. No proxy point exists for it because Spanish nouns are cited bare. This is the strongest thing the track does that the proxy cannot see.

points.label: the adjective agreeing with its noun in gender, number and case
points.note: Taught on ONE adjective, bonus, in three greetings: bonam noctem (fem. acc.), bonum vesperum (masc. acc.), bonam vesperam (the feminine alternate). The agreement is genuinely worked, and it is worked on a single word.

points.label: qualifying adjectives in attributive use, beyond the greeting formulas
points.note: Six colour adjectives are taught (niger, albus, ruber, caeruleus, viridis, flavus) and not one is ever attached to a noun. magnus, parvus, novus, bonus outside the greetings: absent.

points.label: the adjective used predicatively
points.note: sum is taught with its full paradigm and no adjective is ever put after it.

points.label: position: the Latin adjective is mobile, and the mobility carries emphasis
points.note: The Spanish point is postnominal-and-restrictive. Latin word order is free and adjective position is a stylistic instrument rather than a rule, which is a HARDER demand than the proxy makes, and the corpus never raises it.

points.label: relational adjectives: the gentilic
points.note: Romanus, Graecus, Latinus: none of them. The learner cannot say which people they belong to, or that the language they are reading is Latin.

points.label: degree: valde, and the -issimus superlative
points.note: valde returns zero occurrences in 112 files and no superlative is formed anywhere. bene is taught (chapter 27) and is never modified.

points.category: Articulus (the article Latin has not got)
points.label: Latin has NO article, definite or indefinite, and a reader must supply one
points.note: THREE PROXY POINTS COLLAPSE INTO ONE FACT, and the fact is never stated. domus is a house, the house or just house depending on the sentence, and a learner coming from English or Spanish will look for the missing word. The track teaches twenty-five nouns without once saying that the article they are used to is not coming. Restated rather than dropped, exactly as Tamil's inventory restates the same absence.

points.category: Articulus (the article Latin has not got)
points.label: the fused preposition: mecum, tecum, nobiscum
points.note: The Spanish point is al and del, a preposition contracting with an article. Latin has no article to contract with, and its nearest counterpart is the preposition cum enclitic on a pronoun -- mecum, tecum. Absent from the corpus; cum returns zero occurrences in 112 files in any use.

points.label: the demonstrative forms: hic, iste, ille
points.note: hic and ille both return ZERO occurrences in 112 files. Latin's three-way system is the ancestor of the Spanish three-way system the proxy point describes, so the demand transfers exactly, and nothing meets it.

points.label: spatial deixis: near me, near you, over there
points.note: Absent. This is the one place in the inventory where the Spanish point can be taken over word for word, because este/ese/aquel descends from hic/iste/ille.

points.label: the demonstrative agreeing with its noun, and standing alone as a pronoun
points.note: The Spanish point says the demonstrative cannot take an article; in Latin there is no article to exclude, and the demand behind it -- that the demonstrative declines with its noun and can also stand alone -- is what a reader actually needs. Absent.

points.label: the possessive adjectives: meus, tuus
points.note: meus and tuus both return ZERO occurrences in 112 files. The learner CAN say my name is (see LA-A1-POS-03) and cannot say my anything else.

points.label: the possessives for several possessors: noster, vester
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the dative of possession, which is how Latin actually says whose something is
points.note: mihi nomen est, quid tibi nomen est -- literally the name is to me. Chapter 20 is careful about it and even records that Cicero keeps the name nominative while Livy and Sallust pull it into the dative. The Spanish point is about where a possessive stands; the Latin demand behind it is that possession is often a CASE rather than a word, and the corpus teaches exactly that construction and no other.

points.label: cardinal numerals 11 to 20, including subtractive 18 and 19
points.note: duodeviginti and undeviginti, two-from-twenty and one-from-twenty, taught as the genuine Latin oddity the Romance daughters regularised away.

points.label: cardinal numerals above 20
points.note: viginti is the ceiling. Cato's quinque et sexaginta is quoted in chapter 14 and not taught. Roman numerals as a written system are also absent, which is a separate and surprising gap.

points.label: the first three numerals decline, and the rest do not
points.note: unus/una/unum, duo/duae, tres/tria against fixed quattuor and up. Chapter 2 calls it a grammar seed and asks only that the learner notice it.

points.label: ordinal numerals to tenth
points.note: primus, secundus, tertius: absent. Quintilis and Sextilis are taught as month names in chapter 11 with their ordinal sense explained, which is the nearest the corpus comes.

points.label: multus and paucus, agreeing
points.note: Both return zero occurrences.

points.label: satis
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the second person: tu against vos, a pure number contrast with no politeness in it
points.note: Chapter 22 is unusually good on this: Classical Latin's vos carries NO politeness dimension, the polite vous is a Late Latin innovation descended from it, and German's Sie solved the same problem from a different pronoun entirely. A learner who has read this will not import a tu/usted habit.

points.label: the first person: ego, nos
points.note: ego never appears as a word. The -o ending is repeatedly said to BE the I (chapter 1, chapter 24), which is the right teaching and leaves the pronoun itself untaught for the emphatic uses that need it.

points.label: the third person, which Latin builds from a demonstrative
points.note: Latin has no dedicated third-person pronoun and presses is/ea/id into the job. Absent, and behind LA-A1-DEM-01 as well.

points.label: pro-drop: the ending IS the subject
points.note: Stated in chapter 1 on ago, again in chapter 24 on videbo, and demonstrated on every one of the forty-odd verb paradigms. The PCIC A1 grammar column has no slot for it because Spanish inherited the same habit and takes it for granted.

points.label: the accusative object pronoun: te
points.note: te videbo, taught twice, and chapter 24 names te as the direct object in as many words. me is never taught.

points.label: the dative pronoun: mihi, tibi
points.note: mihi nomen est, gratias tibi ago, ignosce mihi. Three separate constructions, all in the first twenty chapters. The Spanish point is the unstressed dative with gustar; Latin's dative is a case rather than a clitic, and the corpus teaches it in three of its commonest jobs.

points.label: the reflexive: se, and the -se verbs
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the relative pronoun qui, quae, quod
points.note: All three forms return ZERO occurrences in 112 files. The single most common word in surviving Latin prose is absent from a track whose declared purpose is reading.

points.label: interrogative pronouns: quis and quid
points.note: quid is taught twice over, in quid agis? and quid tibi nomen est?. quis appears twice in chapter 26 and is not taught, so the WHAT question is available and the WHO question is not.

points.label: the exclamative
points.note: Latin's accusative of exclamation IS taught (chapter 30) and is filed at LA-A1-CAS-04; the exclamative PRONOUN, quantus or qualis, is absent.

points.label: pronouns after a preposition
points.note: No preposition in the corpus takes a pronoun. de mane is quoted and post meridiem is quoted, and both take nouns.

points.label: place deictics: hic, illic
points.note: Absent, with the demonstratives they are built from.

points.label: time deictics: hodie, heri, cras
points.note: cras is taught, in chapter 25's cras te videbo, and hodie and heri both return ZERO occurrences. One third of the set is not the set: a reader who meets heri in a text has nothing to match it against.

points.label: quantity adverbs
points.note: Absent.

points.label: manner adverbs: bene, male
points.note: bene has a whole chapter (27) and male has nothing, so the pair is half taught. valeo answers how one is; there is no way to say that anything went badly.

points.label: polarity: ita and non
points.note: COVERED, AND THE TRACK GOT THERE IN CHAPTER 1. ita (thus, so) and non (not) are taught together as the yes and no Latin does not really have, which is the honest framing. Several tracks in this series cannot say no at all; this one can, on day one.

points.label: connective adverbs: quoque, etiam
points.note: Both absent.

points.label: interrogative adverbs: quomodo, ubi
points.note: quomodo is taught properly, with a chapter of its own (26) tracing it to Italian come, Spanish como and French comment. ubi returns ZERO occurrences, so the learner can ask HOW and cannot ask WHERE. Half a point.

points.label: cur against quia: asking why and answering it
points.note: Spanish spends an A1 point on por que against porque. Latin's pair is cur and quia (or quod), and both members return zero occurrences. The whole causal apparatus is missing; see LA-A1-CJ-11.

points.label: the present indicative, all six persons
points.note: THE TRACK'S GREATEST STRENGTH. Chapters 37 to 43 give roughly forty verbs and the six-person present is set out for them, sum included. Whatever else this inventory reports missing, the learner can conjugate.

points.label: the four conjugations, named as classes
points.note: The paradigms are given verb by verb and the SYSTEM behind them is never named: no lesson says that -are, -ere, -ere and -ire are four families with predictable endings, so a learner meeting an unseen verb has no rule to apply to it. Forty worked examples and no generalisation.

points.label: habeo, eo, do
points.note: Chapter 37's irregulars, matching the ser/estar/haber/ir set the proxy point names.

points.label: the present's values: what is happening and what happens
points.note: Latin's present covers both and has no progressive at all, which is a SMALLER demand than the Spanish point makes and still needs saying, because a learner will look for the missing construction. No lesson says it.

points.label: the imperfect
points.note: Absent. The tense a Latin narrative is mostly written in.

points.label: the perfect
points.note: FOUR PROXY POINTS LAND ON ONE TENSE AND IT IS NOT TAUGHT. Latin's perfect does the work of both Spanish preterite and Spanish present perfect. The corpus mentions tuli and fui inside etymologies (chapters 42 and 37) and teaches neither, so a learner cannot say anything about the past at all -- and the reading construct the caveat names is mostly reading about the past.

points.label: the perfect participle, and the principal parts a dictionary lists
points.note: Every verb here is cited with two principal parts and Latin dictionaries list four. The participle is the third and fourth, and the corpus gives it only for futurus and tuli, in passing.

points.label: the future
points.note: videbo, with the -bo ending named as carrying I will. The PCIC A1 column has no future point at all, so this is enumerated here: the track teaches a tense the proxy does not ask for and does not teach the past, which the proxy asks for four times.

points.label: the imperative
points.note: salve, ave, vale and ignosce are all bare imperatives and chapter 1 says so outright -- Latin does not say hello, it ORDERS you to thrive -- with the singular/plural pair -e against -ete taught alongside. Four imperatives before chapter 5, which is more than most tracks in this series reach at all.

points.label: the infinitive
points.note: Every verb lesson is headed by its infinitive as the form a dictionary lists it under, and chapter 37 says so in as many words.

points.label: the participle used as an adjective
points.note: Latin has no gerund in the Spanish sense; the demand behind the proxy point -- a non-finite form doing adjectival or adverbial work -- lands on the present and perfect participles, and natus is the only participle in the corpus (chapter 14, inside the frozen age formula).

points.label: impersonal verbs with no subject at all
points.note: pluit, ningit, tonat -- chapter 15 gives three and names the pattern. Spanish keeps it for rain and switches to hacer for heat and sun, which the lesson also says, so the point is a genuine Latin demand the proxy's own grammar column cannot state.

points.label: suppletion: one verb built from two unrelated roots
points.note: fero/tuli, and sum/fui named in chapter 37. A reader who does not know that a Latin verb can change root mid-paradigm will not find tuli in a dictionary.

points.label: the case system itself: meaning carried in endings rather than word order
points.note: Chapter 1 states the principle on salve/salvete and calls it the feature that defines Latin. That is the statement; the SYSTEM -- how many cases there are, what each does -- is never set out, which is why the rest of this column is mostly empty.

points.label: the nominative and the accusative, and telling subject from object
points.note: te videbo puts an accusative pronoun in front of a verb and chapter 24 names it as the direct object, which is one instance and not the contrast. No lesson puts a nominative noun and an accusative noun in the same sentence, so the central reading skill -- who is doing what to whom -- is untaught.

points.label: the genitive, and reading it off the dictionary citation
points.note: Every one of the twenty-five nouns in chapters 44 to 47 is cited with its genitive and no lesson says what the genitive MEANS or that it identifies the declension. The form is on the page twenty-five times and its job is never given.

points.label: the accusative of exclamation and wishing
points.note: bonam noctem rather than bona nox, worked twice and with the genuinely attested Felicem natalem quoted beside it.

points.label: the ablative
points.note: Absent. The case with the widest range of jobs in the language, and the corpus does not name it once.

points.label: the vocative, and addressing somebody by name
points.note: No lesson addresses a named person. The meeting scene trades names in the nominative and never calls anyone by one, so salve, Marce is out of reach -- and the vocative is one of the few Latin cases with an ending a beginner can hold.

points.label: free word order, and what it costs a reader
points.note: The corollary of the case system and the thing that most surprises a reader of Latin. Never mentioned; every Latin sentence in the corpus is in an English-like order.

points.label: the affirmative declarative
points.note: valeo, gratias tibi ago, mihi nomen est Marcus. Chapter 19's exchange is five lines long and every one of them is a sentence the learner has built.

points.label: the negative declarative, with non
points.note: non is TAUGHT as a word in chapter 1 and is never once put in front of a verb. The negator is in the learner's hands and the operation is not: non valeo, non intellego and non scio are all unsayable although every part of each is separately taught. A cheaper repair than any other gap in this file.

points.label: yes-or-no questions, with -ne, nonne or num
points.note: Latin marks a polar question with an enclitic particle, which is a demand Spanish does not make at all -- Spanish uses intonation. The corpus teaches no particle and asks no polar question.

points.label: questions with an asking word
points.note: quid agis?, ut vales?, quomodo. Three, all about the person in front of you.

points.label: impersonal existence: est and sunt used to say there is
points.note: est is taught inside mihi nomen est, where it is a copula rather than an existential. Nothing in the corpus says there is.

points.label: copular sentences with sum
points.note: mihi nomen est Marcus. One frame, worked thoroughly.

points.label: transitive and intransitive verbs
points.note: video takes an object in te videbo; sedeo, sto, dormio and curro take none. The contrast is available across chapters 37 to 41 and is never named as a contrast.

points.label: copulative coordination: et, -que, atque
points.note: et occurs TWICE in 112 files and both are inside quoted classical sentences a lesson is discussing -- Cato's quinque et sexaginta annos natus in chapter 14, and valeo et salvos sum recte in chapter 19. It is glossed in passing in the second and taught in neither, and the enclitic -que that a reader meets on every page of Latin prose never appears at all.

points.label: negative coordination: neque, nec
points.note: Zero occurrences, although non itself is taught in chapter 1.

points.label: disjunctive coordination: aut, vel
points.note: Both return ZERO occurrences in 112 files.

points.label: adversative coordination: sed
points.note: sed occurs only inside the Cicero letter quoted in chapter 24 (Sed, ut spero, propediem te videbo), where it is part of the citation and is translated but not taught.

points.label: distributive coordination: alius ... alius
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the infinitive as subject
points.note: Absent. The infinitive is taught only as the citation form.

points.label: the complementary infinitive: volo videre
points.note: Absent, and the modal verbs that take one (volo, possum, debeo) are absent too.

points.label: the accusative and infinitive, which is how Latin reports a thought
points.note: Spanish's point is creo QUE plus a finite clause. Latin does it with an accusative subject and an infinitive, which is one of the two constructions that most confuses a beginning reader, and the corpus never mentions it. cogito is taught as a word in chapter 38 and nothing is ever thought.

points.label: the relative clause
points.note: TWO PROXY POINTS, ONE ABSENCE, AND THE MOST EXPENSIVE ONE IN THIS FILE. qui, quae and quod all return zero occurrences; see LA-A1-PRON-08. A track whose declared purpose is reading cannot read a sentence of connected Latin prose without this.

points.label: causal clauses: quod, quia
points.note: Both zero.

points.label: purpose: ut plus the subjunctive, or ad plus the gerund
points.note: ut appears once, inside the quoted Cicero (ut spero), and the subjunctive is never mentioned in 112 files.

points.label: simultaneity: cum, ubi
points.note: Both zero.

points.label: ask for information about a person
points.note: quid tibi nomen est? and quid agis?. A thing or a place cannot be asked about; see LA-A1-ADV-07 for the missing ubi.

points.label: give personal information: name and age
points.note: mihi nomen est, and viginti annos natus sum -- which chapter 14 points out is NEITHER the Romance have-construction nor the Germanic be-construction but a third one Latin later abandoned. The age answer is capped at twenty by LA-A1-Q-03.

points.label: ask for confirmation with a tag
points.note: nonne and num are the Latin tags and both are absent; see LA-A1-OS-03.

points.label: confirm or deny the previous statement
points.note: ita and non, chapter 1, taught together and taught honestly -- Latin has no bare yes and no, and the lesson says so rather than pretending.

points.label: ask for an opinion by handing the turn back
points.note: B answers and returns ut vales? in chapter 19's exchange, which is the turn-handing move at this level.

points.label: give an opinion
points.note: cogito is taught (chapter 38) and nothing can follow it; see LA-A1-CJ-08.

points.label: ask for an evaluation
points.note: quid agis? and ut vales?, both in chapter 19, and the lesson is careful that the first literally asks what are you doing.

points.label: evaluate with bene
points.note: valeo and bene. The negative half of the scale is missing (LA-A1-ADV-04), so a learner can only ever report that things are going well.

points.label: express approval and disapproval
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express agreement
points.note: ita. Chapter 1 gives the learner the one-word agreement move on the first day.

points.label: express disagreement
points.note: non, as a bare answer. Note the limit: the WORD is available and the OPERATION is not, so a learner can contradict a question and cannot contradict a statement -- see LA-A1-OS-02.

points.label: show scepticism: nescio
points.note: scio is taught in chapter 37 and its negative compound nescio, which is the actual Latin word, is never given -- and non scio cannot be built either, for the reason at LA-A1-OS-02.

points.label: offer a counter-argument
points.note: Needs sed; see LA-A1-CJ-04.

points.label: express possibility
points.note: possum and forsitan are both absent.

points.label: ask whether somebody knows something
points.note: Absent; needs the polar question particle of LA-A1-OS-03.

points.label: express knowledge: scio and the other verb of knowing
points.note: scio, chapter 37, introduced explicitly as one of Latin's TWO verbs for knowing. The other, cognosco or nosco, is never given, so the split Spanish makes with saber and conocer is named and only half filled.

points.label: express ignorance
points.note: See LA-A1-F2-08.

points.label: ask about ability
points.note: Absent, and behind both possum and the polar question.

points.label: express ability
points.note: possum is absent.

points.label: say that you have understood, and that you have not
points.note: THE REPAIR COLUMN, CHECKED SEPARATELY. intellego is taught in chapter 38, and only as a dictionary entry with an etymology (inter plus lego, to read between); it never appears in a sentence, and non intellego cannot be built because negation is never attached to a verb (LA-A1-OS-02). So the commonest thing a beginner has to say is unsayable in both directions. The proxy has no A1 slot for it and CEFR's A1 descriptors do.

points.label: express liking
points.note: amo, chapter 39. Latin has no gustar-style inverted frame at this level -- placet exists and is not taught -- so the demand is restated onto the plain transitive verb of loving, which the corpus does reach.

points.label: ask about a preference by offering alternatives
points.note: Needs aut; see LA-A1-CJ-03.

points.label: express a preference: malo
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express a wish: volo
points.note: Absent. As in the Italian file, this is the single word that would unlock asking, ordering and inviting at this level.

points.label: ask about plans and intentions
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express a plan
points.note: propediem te videbo -- a future, and one attested twice in Cicero's own letters. A thin covering: it is one fixed sentence rather than a productive pattern, and the -bo ending is at least named as carrying I will.

points.label: give an order or instruction
points.note: The imperative is taught in chapter 1 and used again in chapter 4. What is taught are the frozen courtesy imperatives; forming one from a new verb is not modelled.

points.label: ask for something, softened
points.note: quaeso, chapter 3, literally I ask, I beg. THE ITALIAN TRACK HAS NO WORD FOR PLEASE AT ALL AND THIS ONE HAS IT BY CHAPTER 3.

points.label: ask for help
points.note: adiuvo is taught as a dictionary word in chapter 39 and never used; there is no equivalent of the Italian street shout, and no imperative is formed from it.

points.label: respond to a request
points.note: Absent.

points.label: grant permission
points.note: Absent.

points.label: refuse permission
points.note: non is available as a bare answer (LA-A1-F2-07) and nothing softens or explains it.

points.label: offer and invite
points.note: Absent.

points.label: accept an offer
points.note: ita and gratias tibi ago together do this job at A1, and chapter 1 supplies both.

points.label: decline an offer
points.note: Bare non is available and the polite decline (benigne, the Latin no thank you) is not.

points.label: greet
points.note: salve and ave, with the one-listener/many-listeners pair, in chapter 1.

points.label: greet by the time of day
points.note: bonum mane, bonum vesperum, bonam noctem -- and see LA-A1-TES-01, because the track's own lessons say these three are modern pedagogical phrases rather than Roman ones.

points.label: respond to a greeting
points.note: Two worked exchanges, one for wellbeing and one running a whole Roman day from morning to night.

points.label: address somebody by name or title
points.note: No vocative and no title. domine, magister and the rest are absent; see LA-A1-CAS-06.

points.label: introduce a third person
points.note: Absent, and behind the missing demonstrative.

points.label: respond to an introduction
points.note: volup est convenisse, an attested Plautine phrase -- and chapter 21 immediately says it greets a CHANCE ENCOUNTER between people who already know each other, so it is useful and is not a first-introduction formula. Counted covered because the slot has an exponent and the exponent's limits are taught with it, which is better evidence than most points in this file carry.

points.label: apologise
points.note: ignosce mihi, chapter 4. Another courtesy move the Italian track has not got.

points.label: thank, and answer thanks
points.note: gratias tibi ago in chapter 1 and nihil est in chapter 23 -- and chapter 23 states plainly that Classical Latin has NO fixed reply to thanks and that nihil est is a modern conversational convention built from real words. See LA-A1-TES-01.

points.label: offer condolences
points.note: Absent.

points.label: propose a toast
points.note: bene tibi is the Latin toast and is absent, although vinum is taught in chapter 10.

points.label: congratulate
points.note: Felicem natalem is QUOTED in chapter 30 as the attested model for the accusative of wishing, and is not taught as a thing to say. The nearest miss in the social column.

points.label: take leave
points.note: vale and valete, chapter 1, with the imperative named.

points.label: take leave naming when you will meet again
points.note: propediem te videbo and cras te videbo. Chapters 24 and 25, and the honesty label is on each: the first is Cicero's own, the second is built from classical pieces on the same pattern and is not itself attested as a unit.

points.label: greet and respond within a conversation
ask for a person
points.note: Absent.

points.label: show that one is following
points.note: No backchannel of any kind. ita could do it and is never presented that way.

points.label: REPAIR: ask for a repetition
points.note: NOTHING. quid dicis?, iterum, quaeso, lentius: none of them. dico is taught as a dictionary word in chapter 37 and quaeso in chapter 3, so both halves of quid dicis, quaeso? are in the learner's hands and no lesson ever joins them. This track can apologise, thank and say please, and it cannot ask anyone to say something again.

points.label: ask somebody to be quiet
points.note: tace is absent, although the imperative pattern it needs is taught in chapter 1.

points.label: propose closing the conversation
points.note: The day-cycle exchange closes on bonam noctem and vale.

points.label: existence and having: sum and habeo
points.note: Both verbs are taught with full paradigms in chapter 37. Neither is ever given anything to be or to have; see LA-A1-OS-05.

points.label: presence and absence: cum and sine
points.note: Both zero occurrences.

points.label: general quality, with sum
points.note: sum is taught and no quality is ever predicated of anything; see LA-A1-ADJ-03.

points.label: locating an event in time
points.note: Six time nouns are taught (LA-A1-N-03) and nothing is ever placed in one. The ablative of time when, which is the construction, is at LA-A1-CAS-05 and absent.

points.label: certainty and uncertainty
points.note: Absent.

points.label: numerical quantity
points.note: One to twenty.

points.label: relative quantity: plus, minus, multum
points.note: Absent.

points.label: degree
points.note: Absent.

points.label: measures: size, distance and weight
points.note: Absent. Roman measures (pes, milia passuum, libra) are exactly the kind of thing a reader meets early and none is given.

points.label: location: saying where something is
points.note: No locative adverb, no preposition of place used in a sentence, and no ubi to ask with. The learner can name the sea, the earth and the sky and cannot say that anything is in any of them.

points.label: relative position
points.note: Absent.

points.label: distance
points.note: Absent.

points.label: movement and stability
points.note: Six verbs of going, coming, running, walking, standing and sitting, across chapters 37, 40 and 41 -- an unusually complete block, with nowhere to go.

points.label: orientation and direction
points.note: Absent. West is discussed in chapter 33 as the etymological cousin of vesper, which is an etymology and not a direction word.

points.label: order: ordinals, ante and post
points.note: post is quoted inside post meridiem in chapter 35 and never taught; ante is absent; the ordinals are at LA-A1-Q-05.

points.label: origin: where somebody is from
points.note: No gentilic (LA-A1-ADJ-05), no place name (LA-A1-N-02) and no ablative of origin (LA-A1-CAS-05). Three separate gaps, one unanswerable question.

points.label: the clock, and the parts of the day
points.note: COVERED, AND BETTER THAN THE POINT ASKS: chapter 13 teaches hora AND that the Roman hour was not a fixed length, and chapter 35 records that Romans split the day at midday rather than into a separate afternoon, which is why chapter 36 has to explain that there is no good-afternoon greeting.

points.label: locating in time: weekdays, months, seasons
points.note: Seven days as full planet-god phrases, twelve months INCLUDING the original Quintilis and Sextilis, four seasons. The today/yesterday/tomorrow half of the Spanish point is at LA-A1-ADV-02 and is not covered.

points.label: anteriority and posteriority
points.note: Absent; see LA-A1-NG-15.

points.label: sight
points.note: video, chapter 37, and the lesson makes the point that seeing and knowing were once one idea. Latin's track has the verb where the Italian track has only the organ.

points.label: hearing
points.note: audio, chapter 40.

points.label: colour
points.note: Six colour words across chapters 6 and 18, with the honest observation that caeruleus is one of Latin's weakest colour terms.

points.label: open and closed
points.note: aperio and claudo, taught as a matched pair in chapter 41 -- and porta, the thing they act on, in chapter 44.

points.label: general evaluation
points.note: bene is taught and its opposite is not; bonus exists only inside the three greeting formulas and malus never appears. Half a scale.

points.label: value and price
points.note: emo is taught in chapter 43 and there is no money, no price and no way to ask one.

points.label: attractiveness
points.note: Absent.

points.label: quality: bonus and malus
points.note: See LA-A1-NG-25.

points.label: acceptability
points.note: Absent.

points.label: conformity
points.note: ita. Thin, and it is the exponent this level actually uses.

points.label: correctness: right and wrong
points.note: recte is quoted once, inside valeo et salvos sum recte in chapter 19, and is not taught.

points.label: interest
points.note: Absent.

points.label: capacity and competence
points.note: scio. Thin: knowing a thing is not the same as being able to do it, and possum is absent (LA-A1-F2-16). Counted covered because scio IS the Latin word this notion is built on and the corpus teaches it.

points.label: ease and difficulty
points.note: Absent.

points.label: reflection and knowing: the verbs of mind
points.note: cogito, intellego, lego, scio. Chapter 38 is exactly this notion and takes each verb apart -- cogito from shaking together, intellego from reading between.

points.label: verbal expression: saying, speaking and writing
points.note: dico, scribo, respondeo, rogo. Four, and the asking and answering pair are taught as a pair.

points.label: parts of the body
points.note: TWO body words in 112 files -- caput (chapter 8) and manus (chapter 8) -- and the proxy point asks for the set. Compare the Italian track, which teaches nine. This is the cheapest large gain available in the whole file.

points.label: physical characteristics
points.note: Absent.

points.label: actions and positions of the body
points.note: sto, sedeo, dormio, ambulo, curro -- chapters 40 and 41 give five, which is the fullest posture-and-motion block in this series.

points.label: character and personality
points.note: Absent.

points.label: personal data: the name and the age
personal data: the Roman naming system
points.note: praenomen, nomen and cognomen -- the tria nomina -- are what a reader needs to make sense of any Roman name they meet, and the corpus uses Marcus and Iulia without ever explaining the system behind them.

points.label: documents
points.note: Absent. tabula and liber would be the Roman equivalents and neither is taught.

points.label: personal objects
points.note: Absent.

points.label: family relationships
points.note: pater, mater, frater, soror -- four, chapter 7, with the note that Vulgar Latin later abandoned frater and soror for germanus.

points.label: social relationships
points.note: amicus is ABSENT, which is a striking gap: chapter 10 traces panis to companion and to the friendship-word every Romance daughter shares, and never teaches the Latin word for friend.

points.label: celebrations and occasions
points.note: Absent, though Felicem natalem is quoted in chapter 30; see LA-A1-F5-12.

points.label: the meals of the day
points.note: prandium and cena are absent.

points.label: drink
points.note: aqua, vinum, lac.

points.label: foodstuffs
points.note: panis, sal, mel, ovum, piscis -- five, and chapter 47 is built as a table of them.

points.label: dishes and courses
points.note: Absent.

points.label: eating out, or eating at all
points.note: The corpus has eight foodstuffs and NO VERB FOR EATING OR DRINKING. edo and bibo are both absent, so a learner can name bread, salt, honey, egg, fish, water, wine and milk and cannot say what to do with any of them.

points.label: educational institutions
points.note: schola and ludus (in its school sense) are absent -- and ludo, to play, IS taught in chapter 42, which is the same word in its other sense.

points.label: teacher and pupil
points.note: magister and discipulus absent, though puer is quoted inside the chapter 20 grammar frame puero nomen est.

points.label: timetable, examinations and marks
points.note: Absent.

points.label: learning and teaching
points.note: disco and doceo are both absent; lego and intellego are taught and belong to the mind rather than the classroom.

points.label: classroom language
points.note: Nothing; see LA-A1-F6-05.

points.label: teaching materials
points.note: liber, stilus, tabula: absent. For a track about reading, the absence of liber is the one to fix first.

points.label: working activity
points.note: laboro is absent.

points.label: professions and posts
points.note: Absent.

points.label: workplaces and tools
points.note: Absent.

points.label: unemployment and job-seeking
points.note: Absent, and anachronistic in its modern shape; the Roman counterpart a reader meets is the client-patron relation, also absent.

points.label: rights and obligations at work
points.note: Absent.

points.label: what a worker is like
points.note: Absent.

points.label: games and playing
points.note: ludo, chapter 42.

points.label: free time
points.note: otium, the single most characteristically Roman word in this whole notion, is absent.

points.label: shows and spectacles
points.note: Absent.

points.label: sport and the games
points.note: Absent.

points.label: information and communication
points.note: Absent.

points.label: written correspondence
points.note: scribo is taught in chapter 38 and epistula is absent -- and chapter 24 quotes Cicero's own letters twice, so the corpus reads a letter without naming one.

points.label: the printed page, and the Roman book
points.note: liber and volumen are absent; see LA-A1-NE-22.

points.label: housing: the parts of a dwelling
points.note: domus, porta, murus, hortus, focus -- chapter 44 is a whole chapter of them, and domus is taught as the household rather than the walls.

points.label: buying, selling and renting a dwelling
points.note: emo is taught and vendo is not; nothing is ever bought.

points.label: domestic activities
points.note: Absent.

points.label: household objects and furniture
points.note: mensa, lectus, sella: absent. focus, the hearth, is taught (chapter 44) and is the only thing in a Latin house the learner can name.

points.label: the post and messages
points.note: Absent.

points.label: money and banking
points.note: pecunia, argentum, as, denarius: none of them. Two proxy points, one absence.

points.label: health services
points.note: medicus is absent.

points.label: protection and security
points.note: Absent -- and this is the notion a Latin reader meets soonest, in the shape of miles and the army.

points.label: shopping
points.note: emo, chapter 43, taught with the observation that it once meant simply I take.

points.label: clothing
points.note: toga and tunica are absent, which is a surprising omission in a course that spends chapters on Roman daily life.

points.label: payment
points.note: Absent; see LA-A1-NE-41.

points.label: health and illness
points.note: valeo, which is literally to be strong and is the corpus's health word; the lesson makes the link between the greeting and the state explicit. aeger and morbus are absent, so only the well half is sayable.

points.label: centres of health care
points.note: Absent.

points.label: medicine
points.note: Absent.

points.label: hygiene, and the baths
points.note: balneum and aqua-as-washing are absent; aqua is taught only as a drink.

points.label: travel objects and documents
points.note: Absent.

points.label: accommodation
points.note: Absent.

points.label: getting about: roads and ships
points.note: via and navis are absent, and eo, venio and ambulo are all taught, so the corpus has every verb of travel and no road to use one on.

points.label: commerce: the buyer and the seller
points.note: See LA-A1-NE-37.

points.label: businesses and organisations
points.note: Absent.

points.label: craft and industry
points.note: Absent.

points.label: mathematics: the notion of number
points.note: Chapter 2 shows that the first three numerals bend and the rest do not, and chapter 16 takes the subtractive teens apart. That is number as a system rather than a list.

points.label: government and politics
points.note: senatus, consul, res publica, imperator: none of them. For a reading course this is a large hole -- these are among the first nouns in almost any Latin text.

points.label: law and justice
points.note: lex and ius are absent.

points.label: artistic disciplines
points.note: ars is absent.

points.label: music and dance
points.note: Absent.

points.label: architecture, sculpture and painting
points.note: Absent; murus and porta are taught as parts of a house, not as building.

points.label: literature
points.note: lego is taught and poeta, carmen and fabula are absent. Plautus and Cicero are both quoted by name in chapters 21 and 24, so the corpus reads literature and does not name it.

points.label: theatre
points.note: theatrum is absent, though chapter 21's phrase is Plautine and the lesson says so.

points.label: religion
points.note: deus, templum, sacrum: absent. The corpus names Luna, Mars, Mercurius, Iuppiter, Venus, Saturnus and Sol in chapter 5 and names them as PLANETS behind the weekdays rather than as gods, so a reader has met seven Roman deities and been told nothing about Roman religion.

points.label: the universe and the sky
points.note: caelum, lux, stella, luna -- chapters 45 and 46. Better covered than in any other track in this series.

points.label: country, town and city
points.note: urbs, oppidum, patria: absent. For a course whose subject is Rome, the absence of urbs is worth naming twice.

points.label: urban and rural spaces
points.note: hortus and terra. Thin, and they are the two the proxy point is really about.

points.label: climate and weather
points.note: tempestas, pluit, calor, sol, ventus. Chapter 15 also records the sense-shift -- tempestas narrowed to storm while tempus widened to weather -- which is more than the point asks.

points.label: fauna
points.note: canis, feles, cattus and piscis, with the observation that feles was Classical Latin's own word for cat and cattus the newcomer that pushed it out.

points.label: flora
points.note: arbor, flos, herba: absent. hortus is taught as an enclosed piece of ground and nothing grows in it.

points.label: fire, earth, sea and wind
points.note: terra, ignis, ventus, mare, umbra, somnus. Chapter 45 and 46 give ten concrete world nouns between them, which is the track's second-strongest lexical block after the verbs.

points.label: the Latin alphabet, and the letters it does not have
points.note: The Roman alphabet had no J, no U as distinct from V, and no W, and modern editions add them. Chapter 1's pronunciation note says V is a W SOUND, which is the phonetic half; the letter inventory itself, and the fact that Iulia and Iuppiter are spelled with I, is never stated. Nothing in the track names the letters.

points.label: the vowels, and that vowel LENGTH is phonemic
points.note: Every word in the corpus is written with its macrons and the chapter 1 pronunciation notes carry the sound tag macron-long-vowel. Latin's five vowels each come in two lengths, which is a demand Spanish's five-for-five system does not make at all.

points.label: the macron: a length mark, not an accent
points.note: Spanish's accentuation rules mark an EXCEPTION to a stress rule. The macron marks length, and length is what DETERMINES Latin stress, so the demand is inverted and larger. The corpus writes macrons everywhere and its writing lessons score them (the chapter 1 dictation marks the answer wrong without the macron on salve), which is the strongest evidence in this column.

points.label: the macron as the thing that separates two spellings
points.note: Latin's exact counterpart of the Spanish diacritic tilde, and a bigger one: malum is an evil and malum an apple; populus a people and populus a poplar; puella is a nominative and puella an ablative. The corpus writes macrons faithfully and never once says that a macron can be the ONLY thing telling two words apart.

points.label: the consonants, and the reconstructed classical pronunciation
points.note: v as w, c always hard, ti as tee. Taught as named sound tags on the chapter 1 greetings, and the assessment spec names the reconstructed classical model as the default.

points.label: capital letters, and lower-case where Latin differs
points.note: Modern editions capitalise proper nouns; Roman inscriptions were entirely capital and Roman manuscripts entirely minuscule, and neither had the distinction at all. Never stated. The corpus does capitalise the month names and the planet-gods, correctly, without saying that this is an editorial convention.

points.label: syllable division, and where the stress falls
points.note: The penultimate rule -- stress the second-last syllable if it is heavy, otherwise the third-last -- is the one rule that lets a reader say any Latin word aloud, and the corpus gives stress word by word in respellings and never states the rule behind them.

points.label: the punctuation of a modern edition is EDITORIAL, not Roman
points.note: NINE PROXY POINTS COLLAPSE INTO ONE FACT AND THE FACT IS THE INTERESTING PART. Classical Latin was written in scriptio continua with no punctuation, no word spaces and no lower case; every full stop, comma and question mark a reader sees is a modern editor's decision. That is a genuine A1 reading demand and no lesson in 112 files mentions it. The Spanish column's inverted question mark has no Latin counterpart and is restated here as part of the same fact rather than dropped.

points.label: Roman numerals
points.note: I, V, X, L, C, D, M. Twenty cardinal numbers are taught as WORDS and their written form is never given, so a learner who can say viginti cannot read XX.

points.label: abbreviations and initialisms
points.note: S.P.D., cos., D.M., SPQR. Roman abbreviation is by truncation and by initial, and a reader meets it on the first inscription they look at. Absent.

points.category: Lectio (the reading construct this ladder cannot measure)
points.label: THIS INVENTORY MEASURES THE WRONG CONSTRUCT, AND SAYS SO
points.note: core/exam-levels.json's caveat for latin is load-bearing and this point exists to carry it: CEFR is built around communicative can-do statements, Latin is learned almost entirely for READING, and A1 here has been defined as can greet, introduce oneself and read a short exchange. The 54 functional points above ask what a candidate can say to a living interlocutor, and Latin has no living-speaker construct -- exam-levels.json records exam 'no modern proficiency exam', and latin/assessment-spec.md is explicit that Euroclassica's ELEX is not a four-skill pre-A1-to-C2 ladder and that no equivalence is claimed. So the functional column is enumerated because the shared spine requires it and NOT because it is the right measure of this track. Deliberately uncovered, following the precedent of the Sanskrit inventory's point about the pariksha it cannot measure. A reading-only ladder would fit Latin better and the caveat says so; until one exists, read every functional number in this file as a measure of something Latin was not learned for.

points.category: Lectio (the reading construct this ladder cannot measure)
points.label: read a short connected passage of unadapted Latin
points.note: The reading skill this track exists for, and the thing it is furthest from. Two Cicero clauses (chapter 24) and one Plautine phrase (chapter 21) are the only connected classical Latin in 112 files, and both are quoted for discussion rather than read. Nothing longer than a five-line constructed exchange appears anywhere.

points.category: Lectio (the reading construct this ladder cannot measure)
points.label: parse an unseen form: recognise the verb behind a shape you have not met
points.note: Forty verb paradigms are given (LA-A1-V-01) and the four conjugations are never named as classes (LA-A1-V-02), so a learner who meets amabat has no route back to amo. This is the single skill that separates a reader from a phrasebook user, and it is the one the corpus does not build.

points.category: Lectio (the reading construct this ladder cannot measure)
points.label: use a Latin dictionary: find a word from a form on the page
points.note: COVERED, AND IT IS THE READING SKILL THE TRACK ACTUALLY DELIVERS. Every noun is cited with its genitive and every verb with its infinitive, without exception, across 112 lessons -- so a learner who has read this track knows what a dictionary headword looks like and what the second form is for, even though nobody ever tells them what the genitive means (LA-A1-CAS-03).

points.label: tell an attested phrase from a modern pedagogical one
points.note: THE BEST THING THIS TRACK DOES AND NO PROXY POINT EXISTS FOR IT. A dead language taught conversationally invents phrases, and this corpus labels its own inventions: bonam noctem, bonum mane and bonum vesperum are marked as modern pedagogical formulas built on real grammar; nihil est is marked a modern conversational convention with no classical citation for that job; cras te videbo is marked as built from classical pieces on an attested pattern but not itself attested as a unit; and propediem te videbo is marked as Cicero's own, twice, with the letters named. An A1 learner who has read these lessons knows which of their own sentences a Roman would have recognised. Enumerated as latinSpecific because it is a demand only a dead language makes.

points.label: know when the corpus has NO phrase for a slot, and why
points.note: Chapter 36 spends two lessons explaining that there is no good-afternoon greeting because Latin has no simplex afternoon noun and salve works at any hour; chapter 21 explains that the Plautine meeting phrase greets people who already know each other. Refusing to invent a formula and saying why is a teachable move and the track makes it three times.

points.label: know which Latin is being taught: Classical, and what that excludes
points.note: All 112 lessons declare variety: classical, and latin/assessment-spec.md names Classical Latin as the assessed variety with post-classical and Neo-Latin introduced only where a task labels them. No LESSON ever tells the learner this. A reader who meets Ecclesiastical or Medieval Latin -- different pronunciation, different spelling, different vocabulary -- has been given nothing to place it with. This point was measured from the frontmatter and the spec, not imported.
